questions.q: Why is funding a zero trust program harder than funding a typical product project, according to this lesson?
options: Because security staff cost more than engineering staff
Because executives never fund risk reduction of any kind
Because a working foundational-year program is mostly invisible — no outage, no breach, no headline — making it hard to put a dollar value on in a slide deck
Because zero trust has no measurable outcomes at all
questions.explain: Unlike a project with a demo or launch date, a zero trust program's foundational-year success looks like nothing happening, which is genuinely harder to justify in a budget conversation even though it's the intended outcome.

questions.q: What does 'incident cost avoidance' framing actually quantify?
options: The exact date a breach will occur
How much smaller and cheaper future incidents become, not a promise of zero incidents
The total revenue the security team generates
The number of compliance certificates obtained
questions.explain: The framing quantifies a reduced blast radius and reduced future incident cost — it is explicitly not a promise that incidents will stop happening.

questions.q: Why does the lesson prefer tying risk to metrics the business already tracks, like downtime hours or audit findings?
options: Because those metrics are required by law in every jurisdiction
Because new security-specific metrics are always more accurate
Because downtime hours are the only metric executives understand
Because it connects the ask to numbers the organization already recognizes, instead of inventing new ones nobody outside the security team knows
questions.explain: Reusing metrics the business already reports on makes the business case legible to people who don't track security-specific numbers day to day.

questions.q: What are the four parts of a business case that 'survives scrutiny,' per this lesson?
options: The specific gap, the cost of the status quo, the fix's cost/timeline, and the metric that proves it worked
The vendor name, the contract length, the list price, and the renewal date
The CISO's title, their tenure, their certifications, and their direct reports
The marketing name of the product, its logo, and its press release
questions.explain: A business case names the gap in business terms, the realistic cost of leaving it as-is, the phased cost and timeline of the fix, and the metric that will later prove it actually worked.

questions.q: Why is 'we need micro-segmentation' described as a weak budget pitch?
options: Because micro-segmentation is never actually necessary
Because it is too technically detailed for any executive to evaluate
Because it names a product rather than the consequence it changes, giving the committee nothing concrete to approve or later check
Because segmentation projects always fail to ship on schedule
questions.explain: Naming the control instead of the consequence — like the blast radius it reduces — leaves the committee with no concrete number to approve against or verify afterward.
